locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: Parsley

source_text:
THIS is so well known, that it needs no description.

_Government and virtues._] It is under the dominion of Mercury; is very
comfortable to the stomach; helps to provoke urine and women’s courses,
to break wind both in the stomach and bowels, and doth a little open
the body, but the root much more. It opens obstructions both of liver
and spleen, and is therefore accounted one of the five opening roots.
Galen commended it against the falling sickness, and to provoke urine
mightily; especially if the roots be boiled, and eaten like Parsnips.
The seed is effectual to provoke urine and women’s courses, to expel
wind, to break the stone, and ease the pains and torments thereof;
it is also effectual against the venom of any poisonous creature,
and the danger that comes to them that have the lethargy, and is as
good against the cough. The distilled water of Parsley is a familiar
medicine with nurses to give their children when they are troubled
with wind in the stomach or belly which they call the frets; and is
also much available to them that are of great years. The leaves of
Parsley laid to the eyes that are inflamed with heat, or swollen, doth
much help them, if it be used with bread or meal; and being fried
with butter, and applied to women’s breasts that are hard through the
curdling of their milk, it abates the hardness quickly; and also takes
away black and blue marks coming of bruises or falls. The juice thereof
dropped into the ears with a little wine, eases the pains. Tragus sets
down an excellent medicine to help the jaundice and falling sickness,
the dropsy, and stone in the kidneys, in this manner: Take of the seed
of Parsley, Fennel, Annise and Carraways, of each an ounce; of the
roots of Parsley, Burnet, Saxifrage, and Carraways, of each an ounce
and an half; let the seeds be bruised, and the roots washed and cut
small; let them lie all night to steep in a bottle of white wine, and
in the morning be boiled in a close earthen vessel until a third part
or more be wasted; which being strained and cleared, take four ounces
thereof morning and evening first and last, abstaining from drink after
it for three hours. This opens obstructions of the liver and spleen,
and expels the dropsy and jaundice by urine.

    PARSLEY PIERT, OR PARSLEY BREAK

pubmed.title: Parsley.
pubmed.relevance_note: Reviews diuretic effects relevant to urinary retention and general digestive support.

pubmed.title: Petroselinum crispum (Mill.) Fuss (Parsley): An Updated Review of the Traditional Uses, Phytochemistry, and Pharmacology.
pubmed.relevance_note: Comprehensive review covering traditional uses including digestive aid and potential effects on reproductive health.

pubmed.title: Renal health benefits and therapeutic effects of parsley (Petroselinum crispum): a review.
pubmed.relevance_note: Specifically evaluates evidence for renal health and diuretic properties supporting urinary retention claims.

evidence.summary: Modern literature supports parsley's traditional use as a diuretic for urinary retention and digestive aid. Evidence regarding uterine effects (amenorrhea) or specific organ stoppage is less robust, often relying on historical context rather than clinical trials.

pubmed.title: [D-mannitol from Torilis arvensis (Huds.), Link].
pubmed.relevance_note: Identifies D-mannitol as a constituent; no clinical data supports traditional uses for digestive, neurological, or reproductive conditions.

evidence.summary: Modern literature identifies D-mannitol in Torilis arvensis but offers no evidence supporting its traditional use for wind, liver/spleen obstruction, epilepsy, or urinary/menstrual issues. The 2021 retrieved document is unrelated to pharmacology.

concordance.rationale: Modern reviews (PMID: 38189231) confirm diuretic effects supporting urination claims. Carminative properties support wind relief. No evidence supports epilepsy, liver/spleen obstruction, or antivenom uses.
concordance.uncertainty: Evidence for historical claims varies; some are pharmacologically plausible while others lack modern validation.
caveats: Claims regarding epilepsy and antivenom are unsupported by current science.
Safety concerns exist for high-dose consumption in specific populations.

issues: Unearned Grade B: The concordance grade 'B' with a 'partial' direction is unjustified because the entry explicitly flags one of the primary claims ('urination') as having failed verification. A claim that has been mechanically confirmed as false (via `quotes_failed`) should not contribute to a positive or partially positive grade without significant qualification or a downgrade to 'C'/'D' reflecting the partial failure. The rationale cites support for diuretic effects but ignores the specific failure of the quote regarding 'women's courses', creating an incomplete assessment of the evidence base.
